title: Chris Wood: India Wins the 'Reverse AI Trade', Energy Hedges the Iran Risk
excerpt: In his latest GREED & fear note, Jefferies' Chris Wood argues the AI spending cycle has peaked and foreign money is rotating into India - while fresh US-Iran tensions are the biggest risk to the trade.
body:
• Jefferies strategist Chris Wood argues the AI capital-spending cycle has peaked, with hyperscaler returns on invested capital forecast to fall from a 27.2% median in 2024 to as low as 15.7% by 2028.
  • Foreign investors bought a net $7.2 billion of Indian equities over three weeks, including a record $5.2 billion in the week ended November 6, Jefferies says.
  • Jefferies raised India's weighting in its Asia-Pacific ex-Japan portfolio by 2 percentage points to 14% on November 9, cutting South Korea and Taiwan.
  • For India portfolios, Wood's named risk is geopolitical: fresh US-Iran tensions pushing oil higher. His suggested hedge is energy stocks.

India is the standout beneficiary of a global rotation out of artificial-intelligence stocks, according to Chris Wood, Jefferies' global head of equity strategy, whose latest GREED & fear note argues that the AI capital-expenditure cycle has peaked. Wood frames India as a winner of what NDTV Profit described as the "reverse AI trade" - money leaving crowded AI positions for markets whose earnings are driven by domestic demand rather than hyperscaler budgets. The note pairs that optimism with a warning: fresh US-Iran tensions are, in the Economic Times' account of the report, the biggest risk to India, and the sector Wood points to as the hedge is energy.

"The turn is visible in the domestic data too: foreign investors pumped Rs 84,290 crore into Indian stocks in November's first fortnight ."

The AI math behind the call

Wood's case rests on returns, not spending levels. AI capital expenditure is forecast to reach just shy of $1 trillion this year, and consensus expectations for 2027 run to about $1.6 trillion overall, with roughly $1.04 trillion of that from Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta alone, according to consensus estimates cited by Jefferies. Yet the predicted return on that investment is falling: the median return on invested capital for the hyperscalers was 27.2% in 2024 and is expected to drop as low as 15.7% by 2028, Wood and his colleague Desh Peramunetilleke observe. The four largest hyperscalers' forward price-earnings multiple has already fallen from around 30 times in the summer of 2023 to around 21 times. Wood, who favours what he calls disciplined deployment over indiscriminate spending, argues a slowdown could deter "malinvestment" rather than end the AI story - and notes that pharmaceutical stocks, one non-AI beneficiary, have outperformed AI and big-data stocks by 31% since early October, according to MarketWatch's account of the note.

Why India, and why now

The flows have already turned. Foreign investors bought a net $7.2 billion of Indian equities over three weeks, including a record $5.2 billion in the week ended November 6, Jefferies says - a sharp reversal after $32.4 billion of withdrawals since the start of 2026. The turn is visible in the domestic data too: foreign investors pumped Rs 84,290 crore into Indian stocks in November's first fortnight. Jefferies points to valuations it considers modest by recent standards - the Nifty at about 18 times forward earnings - resilient domestic demand, with mutual fund equity inflows of Rs 350 billion in October and Rs 3.9 trillion over the first ten months of 2026, and a private investment recovery tracked through machinery imports, which rose from $29 billion in FY21 to $67 billion in the 12 months to September 2026. On November 9, Jefferies put the view into its model portfolio, raising India's recommended weighting in its Asia-Pacific ex-Japan relative-return portfolio by 2 percentage points to 14%, an overweight against India's 12% weight in the MSCI benchmark, while cutting South Korea to 18% and Taiwan to 24%, both underweight, IANS reported.

The risk: Iran, oil and the energy hedge

Wood's caution is geopolitical. He worries that a lame-duck US president may turn to foreign policy, where he faces fewer constraints, and argues that the resulting risk to investors can only be hedged through energy stocks; he recommends Petrobras, whose US-listed depositary receipts have fallen by a third since October 23. In the GREED & fear India portfolio, he has also raised the weighting of energy stocks by four percentage points this week. "The best hedge for this Iran risk in the portfolio is energy stocks, and we have increased the weighting of energy stocks in our India portfolio this week," he told a Jefferies event on Thursday, the Economic Times reported. For India the channel is direct: an oil-price spike driven by US-Iran tensions raises the energy import bill of one of the world's largest crude importers and pressures the currency and inflation - the reason the Economic Times' report of the note leads with Iran as the biggest risk to the India trade.

What to watch

Three things will test the thesis: whether hyperscaler return forecasts keep sliding as 2027 spending plans are confirmed, whether the foreign buying of the past three weeks persists beyond a short covering burst, and the oil price. Wood's view is a strategist's call, not a result - but the portfolio shift and the flow data mean it is a call money is already acting on.
